guide.summary: Unit 3 covers designing and writing classes: encapsulation with private instance variables, constructors, accessor and mutator methods, toString, methods with parameters and return values, the this keyword, static variables and methods, variable scope, how parameters are passed, preconditions and postconditions, and the ethical and social implications of programs.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a class
sections.body: A class declares instance variables (attributes) and methods (behaviors). Instance variables should be private to enforce encapsulation; access them through public methods. A constructor has the class's name and no return type; it initializes instance variables. If no constructor is written, Java supplies a default no-argument constructor. Accessor (getter) methods return values of instance variables; mutator (setter) methods change them, often with validation. A toString method returns a String representation used by System.out.println.

sections.heading: Methods, this, and scope
sections.body: A method header lists access, return type, name, and parameters. Local variables and parameters exist only within their method or block. When a parameter has the same name as an instance variable, the parameter shadows it; use this.name to refer to the instance variable. Java passes copies of values: modifying a primitive parameter doesn't affect the caller, but a reference parameter refers to the same object, so mutating that object is visible to the caller (reassigning the parameter is not).

sections.heading: Static members and design
sections.body: Static variables belong to the class and are shared by all instances (e.g., a counter of objects created). Static methods can't access instance variables or call instance methods without an object, and can't use this. Preconditions state what must be true before a method is called; postconditions state what is true after. Good design decomposes problems into smaller methods. Programs have ethical and social consequences, including privacy, bias in data and algorithms, and intellectual property.

keyTakeaways: Instance variables private; methods public as needed.
Constructors initialize state and have no return type.
this.x refers to the instance variable when shadowed.
Primitives are passed by value; object references are copied.
Static variables are shared across all objects.
Static methods can't use instance variables directly.
commonMistakes: Writing a return type on a constructor (it becomes a regular method).
Assigning a parameter to itself (x = x) instead of this.x = x.
Declaring a local variable that shadows an instance variable in the constructor.
Accessing private variables of another class directly.
Calling an instance method from a static method without an object.
examTips: FRQ Q2: match the specified method names, parameter types, and return types exactly.
Trace object state after each method call in MCQs.
Watch for constructors that accidentally declare local variables.
For static counters, remember every constructor call updates the shared value.
guide.cramSheet:
**Class:** private fields · public constructor · accessors · mutators · toString

**Constructor:** same name, no return type · initializes fields

**this:** this.x = x for shadowed names

**Passing:** primitives copied · references copied (object shared)

**Static:** shared by class · static methods: no this, no instance fields

**Design:** pre/postconditions · decomposition · ethics (privacy, bias)

practice.stem: A class Student has a private int field credits. Which method correctly adds earned credits only when the argument is positive?

choices.text: public void addCredits(int c) { if (c > 0) { credits += c; } }
public int addCredits(int c) { credits + c; }
private void addCredits(int c) { credits = c; }
public static void addCredits(int c) { credits += c; }

practice.explanation: B doesn't compile (no assignment or return), C replaces instead of adding and is private, D is static and can't access credits.
this.a = b sets the field a to 8. b = a assigns the parameter b the value of parameter a (3); the field b stays 0.

distractors.B: Thinks b = a sets the field.

distractors.C: Counts each toggle to 'on' without decrements.

practice.topic: Ethical and Social Implications of Computing
practice.stem: A loan-approval program is trained on historical data in which certain neighborhoods were denied loans unfairly. Which concern is most directly raised?

choices.text: The program may reproduce past bias, unfairly denying loans to applicants from those neighborhoods.
The program will run too slowly.
The program violates encapsulation.
The program cannot be written in Java.

practice.explanation: Algorithms trained on biased data can perpetuate discrimination.

practice.prompt:
Write the complete class `GymMembership`. A membership has a member name and a number of visits remaining.

- The constructor takes the member's name and an initial number of visits.
- `getName()` returns the name.
- `getVisitsLeft()` returns the visits remaining.
- `checkIn()` returns true and decreases visits by 1 if at least one visit remains; otherwise it returns false and changes nothing.
- `addVisits(int n)` adds n visits if n is positive. In addition, every time the total visits purchased through addVisits reaches a new multiple of 10 (10, 20, 30, …), the member receives 1 bonus visit.

Example: a membership created with 2 visits; addVisits(6) → 8 visits left (6 purchased total); addVisits(5) → 11 purchased total, crossing 10, so 8 + 5 + 1 = 14 visits left.

rubric.description: public class GymMembership with private instance variables for name, visits left, and total purchased.
Constructor with String and int parameters initializes name and visits (and purchased to 0).
getName and getVisitsLeft return the correct fields.
Decrements and returns true; otherwise returns false without change.
Adds n to visits and to the purchased total only when n > 0.
Awards one bonus visit for each new multiple of 10 crossed (e.g., compares purchased / 10 before and after).
